Three old air bubbles sit trapped high in the glass's curve at the top of frame, catching a warm light beyond as tiny amber moons, each a different size.
A hairline crack runs across the curve at the top of frame, mended long ago with a fine seam of gold that catches the light in one sharp bright edge.
The water has gone faintly amber with age, washing the whole interior in the colour of old honey and warm afternoon light.
A soft constellation of tiny scratches rings the glass at the bottom curve, worn pale and bright where ten thousand thumbs have lifted and set it down.
The glass runs thick and faintly green at the very rim, the way old harbour glass is, bending the edge of the world into cool jade.
One bright warm highlight rides the curve at the upper left of frame, a hard white comma of light laid over the amber world behind it.
The lit windows of the far street repeat around the curve as a loose smear of warm amber dots, each one a ghost of the original.
At the extreme right edge of frame the glass turns away and the whole world stretches and bends, the rooftops pulling long and dreamlike.
The scene doubles faintly in the glass's thickness, the steeple appearing twice — once sharp, once a pale echo half a degree to the left.
A cold blue rim-light runs along the curve at the very top of frame, thin as a wire and bright as a struck flint.
A flaw in the glass catches the world's brightest light and throws a small six-pointed star of flare across the upper corner of the frame.
A band of dark walnut, strong as tea, runs along the very bottom edge of the frame, worn to a warm pale stripe where thumbs have rested for decades.
A black-painted cast-iron base sits as a narrow band along the bottom of frame, its scalloped foot just visible, carrying one small painted fish in cadmium red.
The brass top of the base runs polished and mirror-bright along the bottom edge of the picture, the grooves below it gone deep verdigris green.
The band along the bottom edge of the frame blazes strong post-box red at one end and has faded to dusty pink at the other, sun-bleached on one side only.
Ribbed cream porcelain forms the base's visible sliver, one scallop along the bottom edge wearing a small clean chip that shows the buff clay beneath.
At the lower right of frame a little winding key's shaft crosses the very corner, rubbed to a silver brightness, one fine line of gear-teeth catching light behind it.
Along the bottom edge a thin strip of green baize has lifted away and curls upward into a soft dark scroll at the frame's lowest corner.
A band of hand-painted cobalt runs along the bottom edge of the frame, the brushstrokes still readable across it as loose confident arcs.
At the bottom left corner a sliver of pale birch meets a sliver of dark walnut, two mismatched pieces fitted together long ago and each still its own bare colour.
A bubble trapped in the curve has drifted over the years to rest against the glass at the right of frame, glowing faintly gold in the amber water.
The gold mend across the crack widens at one end into the thinnest possible fork, bright as a cracked egg held to the light, high at the top of frame.
Where the glass meets the base a thin ring of old sealant has gone amber and slightly crystalline, catching the warm lamp as a broken circle of sparks.
A single painted sun sits on the band along the bottom edge of the frame — eight straight rays, cadmium yellow, barely a centimetre wide, slightly crooked.
The glass at the extreme top of frame runs thick and slightly rippled, the way it goes when it has been mouth-blown, softening everything just behind it.
